== APPRAISAL INSTRUCTIONS (GEMINI_HANDOFF_BRIEF §3 Task D; RISK_OF_BIAS.md §§1-2; APPRAISAL_FORM.md; CODEBOOK.md §8) ==
1. ACCESSIBILITY GATE:

NEVER guess study design or bias ratings from citation/title!

2. STEP 1 — INDEPENDENT DESIGN CLASSIFICATION & TOOL SELECTION (`RISK_OF_BIAS.md` §1):
   Classify the study's actual design from its Methods section, then select the matching appraisal tool:
   - `"RoB 2 (parallel-trial variant)"`: Individually randomized controlled trial. Rate all 5 domains (`D1` Randomization process; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"RoB 2 (cluster-randomized trials variant)"`: Cluster-randomized trial (villages, compounds, neighbourhoods, schools, utilities randomized as clusters). Rate all 6 domains (`D1a` Randomization process; `D1b` Timing of identification or recruitment of participants within clusters; `D2` Deviations from intended interventions; `D3` Missing outcome data; `D4` Measurement of the outcome; `D5` Selection of the reported result) as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`, and overall rating as `"Low"`, `"Some concerns"`, or `"High"`.
   - `"ROBINS-I"`: Non-randomized study of an intervention / policy with a genuine comparator (DiD, IV, RDD, PSM, ITS, controlled before-after, comparative longitudinal/panel evaluation). Rate all 7 domains (`D1` Bias due to confounding; `D2` Bias in selection of participants into the study; `D3` Bias in classification of interventions; `D4` Bias due to deviations from intended interventions; `D5` Bias due to missing data; `D6` Bias in measurement of outcomes; `D7` Bias in selection of the reported result — note `No information` honestly if no pre-analysis plan/protocol exists) as `"Low"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Serious"`, `"Critical"`, or `"No information"`, and overall rating in the same vocabulary. Do NOT assign single-case histories with no comparator arm to ROBINS-I!
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross Sectional Studies"`: Quantitative cross-sectional survey / observational regression without a quasi-experimental intervention structure. Rate all 8 items (`Q1` Inclusion criteria in sample clearly defined; `Q2` Study subjects and setting described in detail; `Q3` Exposure measured validly and reliably; `Q4` Objective, standard criteria used for measurement of condition; `Q5` Confounding factors identified; `Q6` Strategies to deal with confounding factors stated; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly and reliably; `Q8` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`. Provide overall narrative judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, or `"High concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Cohort Studies"`: Observational comparative cohort design (not framed as a ROBINS-I intervention). Rate all 11 items (`Q1` Similar groups from same population; `Q2` Exposures measured similarly; `Q3` Exposure measured validly/reliably; `Q4` Confounding factors identified; `Q5` Strategies to deal with confounding stated; `Q6` Participants free of outcome at start; `Q7` Outcomes measured validly/reliably; `Q8` Follow-up time reported and sufficient; `Q9` Follow-up complete or loss explored; `Q10` Strategies to address incomplete follow-up utilized; `Q11` Appropriate statistical analysis used) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, `"Unclear"`, or `"Not applicable"`, plus narrative overall judgment (`"Low concern"`, `"Some concern"`, `"High concern"`).
   - `"CASP Qualitative Checklist"`: Primary qualitative study (interviews, ethnography, focus groups, qualitative documentary/field case study). Rate all 10 items (`Q1` Clear statement of aims; `Q2` Qualitative methodology appropriate; `Q3` Research design appropriate to address aims; `Q4` Recruitment strategy appropriate to aims; `Q5` Data collected in a way that addressed research issue; `Q6` Relationship between researcher and participants adequately considered [reflexivity]; `Q7` Ethical issues considered; `Q8` Data analysis sufficiently rigorous; `Q9` Clear statement of findings; `Q10` How valuable is the research [narrative assessment]). Rate Q1-Q9 `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`, and Q10 narratively; give narrative `overall_rating` (e.g. `"Low methodological concern"`, `"Moderate concern (X Can't tell / No items)"`, `"High methodological concern"` — no numeric score).
   - `"MMAT (Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool)"`: Genuine mixed-methods primary study combining qualitative AND quantitative empirical components (do NOT assign purely quantitative or purely qualitative studies to MMAT). Rate Screening `S1`-`S2`, Qualitative `1.1`-`1.5`, the matching Quantitative 5-item block (`2.1`-`2.5` randomized, `3.1`-`3.5` non-randomized, or `4.1`-`4.5` descriptive), AND Mixed-Methods integration `5.1`-`5.5` (`5.1` adequate rationale for mixed methods; `5.2` components effectively integrated; `5.3` outputs of integration adequately interpreted; `5.4` divergences/inconsistencies adequately addressed; `5.5` components adhere to quality criteria of each tradition) as `"Yes"`, `"No"`, or `"Can't tell"`. Per MMAT 2018 rules, NEVER compute a numeric score; provide a concise criterion-grounded narrative `overall_rating` noting that overall quality cannot exceed the weakest component.
   - `"AMSTAR 2"`: Secondary systematic review, meta-analysis, or scoping review with an explicit systematic search/screening method (NEVER apply AMSTAR 2 to non-systematic narrative literature reviews!). Rate all 16 items `Q1`-`Q16` (explicitly marking critical domains `Q2`, `Q4`, `Q7`, `Q9`, `Q11`, `Q13`, `Q15`) as `"Yes"`, `"Partial Yes"` (where applicable), `"No"`, or `"Not applicable (no meta-analysis)"`, and apply AMSTAR 2 overall confidence (`"High"`, `"Moderate"`, `"Low"`, `"Critically Low"`).
   - `"Legal Institutional Evidence Appraisal Framework"`: Doctrinal-empirical hybrid, jurimetric analysis, or institutional/legal-historical case study that fits NONE of the six conventional designs above. Rate all 13 narrative domains (`D1` Legal source accuracy; `D2` Jurisdictional specificity; `D3` Exposure definition; `D4` Outcome definition; `D5` Sampling transparency; `D6` Selection process; `D7` Measurement transparency; `D8` Causal identification; `D9` Treatment of confounding; `D10` Institutional context; `D11` Replication potential; `D12` Coding transparency; `D13` Researcher reflexivity) as `"strong"`, `"adequate"`, `"weak"`, or `"not assessable"`. Explicitly frame `overall_rating` as a structured non-validated judgment (NEVER a numeric composite score!).
   - `"NONE"`: Use when the study fits NONE of the listed instruments (e.g., pure mathematical/simulation optimization model with no empirical sample, or non-systematic narrative essay/review with no primary empirical method and no systematic search). Set `overall_rating = "NOT APPLICABLE (design fits no listed tool)"`, explain clearly in `why_tool_chosen` and `overall_narrative_summary` rather than forcing an inappropriate checklist, and still fill the 7 `cross_tool_domains` honestly from the paper!

raw_response.chosen_tool: JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Cohort Studies

cross_tool_domains.attrition: Some concern: Although prospective wave-to-wave attrition does not occur because life histories were collected retrospectively in 2000, unobserved selection/loss from pre-2000 mortality and international emigration could not be measured or adjusted for, while right-censoring for internal out-migration from Ouagadougou (424 in first-access; 310 in first-loss) relies on an untested non-informative censoring assumption and survey non-response rates are unreported.
cross_tool_domains.confounding: Some concern: Time-varying Cox proportional hazards models adjust for historical decade, sex, education, economic activity, marital status, childhood residence at age 6, housing tenure, urban zoning, and tenure-by-zone interactions, but direct time-varying household income/wealth, connection fees/tariffs, household size, and polygamous compound headship are unmeasured.
cross_tool_domains.legal_measurement_quality: Moderate / coarse proxy quality: Formal municipal allotment/zoning status (which legally governs eligibility for ONEA piped connections) and property tenure are operationalized via respondent-reported residence in three broad spatial zones (downtown, zoned periphery, non-zoned periphery) and four tenure categories (owner/co-owner, renter, parent's residence, other's residence), without verification of formal titles, exact neighbourhood rezoning/allotment dates, or ONEA connection regulations.
cross_tool_domains.measurement_bias: Some concern: Multi-decade life-course exposures and water transitions (from age 6/15 up to age 64) rely on retrospective self-report in a low-literacy setting; an AGEVEN age-event calendar mitigated temporal ordering errors, but recall lapse over decades and projection-based imputation of urban/rural status at age 6 introduce potential misclassification.
cross_tool_domains.outcome_measurement_quality: Moderate: Piped water access (at least one private or shared tap in the dwelling, plot, or yard) and transition dates are systematically tracked across all residence spells lasting >=3 months, distinguishing residential moves from in-situ connections/disconnections, but rely on unverified retrospective recall, conflate exclusive household taps with shared or potentially locked compound taps, and omit service continuity or water quality.
cross_tool_domains.reporting_bias: Some concern: No pre-registered protocol or analysis plan is mentioned; regression tables omit confidence intervals/standard errors and proportional-hazards assumption diagnostics, highlight marginal p < 0.15 effects, and contain an unexplained minor discrepancy in the first-loss sample size between Table 1 (1,226 persons at risk) and text on PDF page 12 (1,220 people).
cross_tool_domains.selection_bias: Some concern: Uses a nationally representative two-stage stratified probability sample (EMIUB 2000) with sampling weights and includes 294 former Ouagadougou residents interviewed elsewhere in Burkina Faso, but retrospective sampling of living residents in 2000 excludes deceased persons and international emigrants (survivor/emigrant selection bias) and omits survey response rates.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Were the two groups similar and recruited from the same population?
domain_ratings.justification: All individuals in both the first-access and first-loss risk sets were drawn from the same nationally representative two-stage stratified probability survey (EMIUB 2000, aged 15-64) covering current Ouagadougou residents (n=2,839) and former Ouagadougou residents interviewed elsewhere in Burkina Faso (n=294), with Ouagadougou sampling weights applied.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Were the exposures measured similarly to assign people to both exposed and unexposed groups?
domain_ratings.justification: Identical retrospective life-history questionnaires and the standardized AGEVEN age-event calendar matrix were administered across all sampled respondents to record residential spells (>=3 months), tenure status, urban zone, employment, and marital status.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was the exposure measured in a valid and reliable way?
domain_ratings.justification: Exposures (tenure status, zone of residence, employment, marital transitions) were collected via structured AGEVEN life-history calendars, which improve temporal ordering, but multi-decade retrospective recall in a low-literacy population remains subject to memory lapse, urban/rural childhood status at age 6 relied on demographic projections (Beauchemin et al., 2002), and zoning/tenure lacked administrative verification.

The authors explicitly identify key demographic, socioeconomic, life-course, spatial, and macro-historical confounders—sex, historical decade (pre-1970 to 1990-2000), education, economic activity sector, marital status, migration origin at age 6, residential tenure status, and urban zoning—though direct household income/wealth was unavailable in retrospective histories.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Were strategies to deal with confounding factors stated?
domain_ratings.justification: Multivariable Cox proportional hazards models (Models 1a/1b and 2a/2b) incorporate time-varying covariates for period, economic activity, marital status, tenure status, and zone of residence, plus tenure-by-zone interaction terms and delayed entry for post-age-15 migrants, though residual confounding from unmeasured time-varying wealth/income and household composition remains.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF pp. 6-8, 11, 14 (Methods; Explanatory Variables; Tables 2 and 5)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Were the groups/participants free of the outcome at the start of the study (or at the moment of exposure)?
domain_ratings.justification: Explicitly enforced by risk-set construction: for first access (n=2,134), anyone already living in a dwelling with piped water at age 15 or upon first arrival in Ouagadougou after age 15 was excluded; conversely, for first loss (n=1,226 in Table 1 / 1,220 in text), all included individuals began observation in a dwelling with piped water.
domain_ratings.where_found: PDF pp. 7, 9, 12 (Methods; Table 1; Access to Piped Water; Loss of Piped Water)

domain_ratings.domain_name: Were the outcomes measured in a valid and reliable way?
domain_ratings.justification: Piped water status (at least one tap in dwelling, plot, or yard) was recorded for the start, end, and any mid-spell transition date of every residence spell >=3 months using an AGEVEN calendar, but relies on unverified retrospective recall over decades and pools exclusive household taps with shared compound taps that may be locked by household heads.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was the follow up time reported and sufficient to be long enough for outcomes to occur?
domain_ratings.justification: Observation spans life-course histories from age 15 up to age 64 across four decades (1960-2000), with total person-time reported in Tables 2 and 5 (255,057 person-time units for first access; 103,963 for first loss) and Kaplan-Meier curves plotted across adulthood, providing ample duration to observe transitions.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Was follow up complete, and if not, were the reasons to loss to follow up described and explored?
domain_ratings.justification: The authors explicitly identify right-censoring due to internal emigration (424 in first access; 310 in first loss) and acknowledge unobserved selection/loss due to pre-2000 mortality and international emigration, but survey response rates are omitted and differential characteristics of deceased or international migrants could not be empirically explored—only assumed similar to interviewees.

domain_ratings.domain_name: Were strategies to address incomplete follow up utilized?
domain_ratings.justification: Including 294 former Ouagadougou residents interviewed elsewhere in Burkina Faso and right-censoring emigration spells in the Cox hazard likelihood mitigated internal out-migration bias, but no statistical adjustment or sensitivity analysis addressed pre-survey mortality, international emigration, or survey non-response.

Kaplan-Meier survivor functions and semi-parametric Cox proportional hazards models handling delayed entry, right-censoring, sampling weights, time-varying covariates, and tenure-by-zone interactions are appropriate for life-course event-history data, despite minor omissions of confidence intervals/standard errors, proportional-hazards tests, and quasi-complete separation (0.00***) in non-zoned periphery cells.

evidence_quotes.quote: The sample is a two-stage stratified probability sample.

For each residence, we have information on the type of water supply at the beginning of the stay in the residence, at the end and, when it occurred, the date of change of type of water supply during the stay in the residence.
For these individuals, we can only hypothesise that they had similar experiences to those of the persons interviewed.

Entry into observation takes two forms: living in Ouagadougou at age 15 in a dwelling without piped water or arriving in Ouagadougou after age 15 and living in a house without piped water. Individuals who are aged 15 years and live in a house with piped water or who upon arrival in Ouagadougou after age 15 live for the first time in a house with piped water are thus excluded from analysis.

evidence_quotes.criterion: Legal/institutional zoning constraint on piped network access (Q3/Q4)
evidence_quotes.page: PDF p. 8 (Data and Methods > Explanatory Variables)
evidence_quotes.quote: The connection to the water system is indeed not possible in non-zoned areas.

evidence_quotes.criterion: Sample size reporting discrepancy vs Table 1 n=1226 (Q11/reporting)
evidence_quotes.page: PDF p. 12 (Results > Loss of Piped Water)
evidence_quotes.quote: In all, this analysis covers a sample of 1220 people: 901 with PW in their first residential unit in Ouagadougou and 319 who had access to PW after having lived in one or more houses without PW.

raw_response.overall_narrative_summary: Some concern (JBI Cohort Studies narrative judgment: 7 Yes, 4 Unclear, 0 No). Dos Santos and LeGrand (2013) analyze retrospective life-history cohorts reconstructed from Burkina Faso's nationally representative 2000 EMIUB survey (2,839 Ouagadougou respondents plus 294 former residents interviewed elsewhere in the country) using Kaplan-Meier curves and time-varying Cox proportional hazards models to estimate time to first access (n=2,134) and first loss (n=1,226 in Table 1; n=1,220 in text) of on-plot piped water. Methodological strengths include probability sampling with national capture of internal out-migrants from Ouagadougou, strict outcome-free baseline risk sets with delayed entry, structured AGEVEN age-event calendars to aid temporal ordering, and explicit modeling of time-varying housing tenure interacted with municipal zoning status (downtown, zoned periphery, non-zoned periphery). Key limitations driving 'Some concern' are multi-decade retrospective recall vulnerability for both exposures and water-transition dates without ONEA utility verification, survivor and international-emigrant selection bias inherent to interviewing living residents in 2000, unmeasured time-varying household income/wealth and connection-cost confounders, pooling of exclusive private taps with shared/potentially locked compound taps, and minor statistical reporting omissions (no confidence intervals/standard errors, no proportional-hazards diagnostics, and a 1,226 vs 1,220 sample-size discrepancy).
raw_response.study_design_identified: Retrospective cohort / life-course event-history survival study (semi-parametric Cox proportional hazards and Kaplan-Meier analysis of longitudinal residential and water-access trajectories reconstructed from a nationally representative 2000 retrospective survey)
raw_response.where_found_summary: Study design, sampling, retrospective recall/survivor-bias discussion, Cox hazard specification, risk-set definitions, and covariates are detailed in 'Data and Methods' (PDF pp. 5-8, Table 1, and Notes 1-7 on PDF p. 17). Empirical survival curves, multivariable hazard ratios, and tenure-by-zone interactions are reported in 'Results' (PDF pp. 8-15, Figures 1-3, Tables 2-7), with institutional context on ONEA and land zoning in 'Water Access in Ouagadougou' (PDF pp. 4-5) and 'Discussion and Conclusion' (PDF pp. 15-17).
raw_response.why_tool_chosen: Although data were gathered in a single-wave 2000 retrospective life-history survey (EMIUB), the empirical design reconstructs longitudinal person-time cohorts starting from an outcome-free state at age 15 (or city arrival after age 15) up to event occurrence or right-censoring, analyzed via Kaplan-Meier survivor curves and time-varying Cox proportional hazards models. There is no discrete policy/intervention evaluation with a comparator arm (ruling out ROBINS-I), making the JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Cohort Studies the best-fitting instrument to evaluate baseline outcome-free status, person-time follow-up, censoring/loss to follow-up, time-varying confounding, and survival modeling.
